subject: S&P turns negative on Meta’s AI spending
bodyMarkdown:
Two central banks turned hawkish on Wednesday, and on Friday a rating agency put a warning label on the biggest AI spender in the world. Those are the same story, and together they set what your mortgage renewal and your index fund will cost you next year.

## S&P turned negative on Meta's buildout

On Friday, S&P Global Ratings moved its outlook on Meta to negative from stable while affirming the AA- rating. The complaint was not weak advertising. S&P now projects Meta's capital spending at roughly $140 billion this year, more than $225 billion in 2027 and $252 billion in 2028, far above its own earlier forecasts, and it expects adjusted leverage to climb from about 0.3 times at the end of this year to 1.3 times by 2028. It put Meta's future lease obligations at $355.7 billion as of September 30. S&P also said Meta's ability to monetize these investments looks more limited than its peers'. An outlook change is not a downgrade, and Meta is nowhere near distress. It is a rating agency saying out loud that it cannot see when the revenue arrives.

## The money got more expensive the same week

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.50% on Wednesday, its first increase since July 2023, and said there could be a need to go further while the Governing Council proceeds carefully. The next decision is December 9. That same day the Fed held its range at 3.75% to 4% on a split vote, with Governor Lisa Cook among two dissenters, and Chair Kevin Warsh said of financial conditions, "I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight." NPR reported that investors now widely expect a hike in December. Both banks spent two years cutting and have now stopped. The Government of Canada five-year yield closed at 3.62% on Wednesday, and that yield sits under every fixed mortgage and every data centre lease signed in this country.

## Credit is moving before the share prices do

I wrote yesterday that October punished the companies funding AI out of debt and rewarded the ones paying from cash flow. Here is the machinery under that. A Seeking Alpha piece published Sunday noted that **credit default swap** spreads on Meta, Broadcom and Nvidia have widened even while their share prices held up (a credit default swap is the contract that pays out if a borrower fails to pay). Cautious money is repricing the debt before the equity market agrees to anything. Meta is filling the gap with stock as well as bonds, announcing a plan to raise about $95 billion, and Investing.com reported in late October that Nvidia would put $3 billion into that offering. A chip supplier helping finance a customer's purchases of its own chips is how vendor financing worked in telecom in 1999, and I doubt anyone involved has forgotten how that ended.

## The takeaway

I have stopped reading AI headlines for demand signals and started reading them for funding terms, because demand is not what is wobbling. Watch whether S&P or Moody's moves next on Oracle, which carries the widest spreads of the big spenders, and watch what the Bank of Canada says on December 9. If you renew a mortgage in 2027, the fixed rate you are quoted will depend partly on how much debt American data centres need that year, which sounds absurd and is true anyway. The buildout does not need to fail to hurt you; it only needs to get more expensive to finance.
